name: Madrid
tagline: Spain's grand capital of art, terraces and golden light.
whenBlurb: Spring and early autumn are ideal, April to June and September to October; avoid July and August when the city empties and bakes.

ourTake.lede: Madrid rewards those who move at its own hours: skip the morning rush at the big museums and go late, then let the city open up over a long lunch and an even longer night. The Prado and Reina Sofía are the anchors, but the real city is in its plazas, its markets, and its unhurried bar culture, so leave room for wandering rather than ticking boxes. Base yourself centrally and treat the day trips to Toledo or Segovia as optional, not obligatory.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a European capital with world-class art, late dinners and a warm, unhurried pace of living.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after beaches, dramatic landscapes or a quiet retreat away from a busy city.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Ritz, Madrid
items.description: The capital's defining address, a Belle Époque palace beside the Prado, restored to its full 1910 grandeur.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Madrid
items.description: Seven heritage buildings woven into one grand house at Canalejas, Four Seasons' first Spanish address, between Sol and the Prado.

items.name: Rosewood Villa Magna
items.description: The Salamanca grande dame reborn, Rosewood's flagship on Madrid's most coveted boulevard, all calm and quiet polish.

items.name: BLESS Hotel Madrid
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A contemporary luxury house on the Golden Mile, in the former Gran Hotel Velázquez, bold, design-led, and gastronomically serious.

items.name: Santo Mauro, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: A duke's 1894 neoclassical mansion turned intimate palace hotel, a marble staircase, a garden, and deep quiet off the Castellana.

items.name: Hotel Único Madrid
items.description: A restored 19th-century Salamanca townhouse turned intimate luxury hotel, on the city's smartest shopping street.

items.name: Gran Meliá Palacio de los Duques
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A 19th-century palace and former 13th-century convent by the Royal Palace, dressed with a Velázquez-inspired hand.

items.name: The Madrid EDITION
items.description: Ian Schrager's cool, light-filled house in the old centre, a rooftop, a pool and a lively scene under one modern roof.

items.name: URSO Hotel & Spa
items.description: A restored Belle Époque palace turned boutique house between Chamberí and Chueca, a Natura Bissé spa and quiet good taste.

items.name: The Principal Madrid
items.description: An early-20th-century building crowned by one of Madrid's great rooftops, at the head of Gran Vía.

items.name: The Westin Palace, Madrid
items.description: A 1912 grand hotel between the Prado and the Thyssen, its stained-glass rotunda one of the city's great rooms.

items.name: Gran Hotel Inglés
items.description: Madrid's oldest luxury hotel, reborn, a jewel-box in the literary quarter, restored with real depth of character.

items.name: Brach Madrid
items.description: Philippe Starck's exuberant, botanical Madrid house, a lush, design-forward stay near the Salamanca boutiques.

items.name: CoolRooms Palacio de Atocha
items.description: A restored palace near Atocha and the Reina Sofía, with a rooftop pool over the old town.

items.name: Only YOU Boutique Hotel Madrid
items.description: A design-led townhouse in the heart of Chueca, warm, sociable and well-placed for the city's most vibrant quarter.

items.name: Only YOU Hotel Atocha
items.description: A polished, contemporary house near Atocha station and the Retiro, easy connections and a rooftop terrace.

items.name: Museo Nacional del Prado
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro, a landscape of Arts and Sciences (2021)
items.description: Spain's crown jewel of a picture gallery: Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and the largest hoard of Bosch and Titian anywhere. Book a private out-of-hours or expert-led tour so a multi-generational family can stand alone before the masterpieces before the crowds arrive.

items.name: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: Home to Picasso's Guernica, which commands its own hushed room, alongside the country's greatest collection of Dalí and Miró. A private guide makes the modern-art narrative land for teenagers and grandparents alike.

items.name: Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: The third point of the Golden Triangle, a former private aristocratic collection that fills the gaps the Prado and Reina Sofía leave, from early Italian gold-ground panels to Hopper and Impressionism. Its scale is human, ideal for a gentle, unhurried afternoon.

items.name: Palacio Real de Madrid (Royal Palace)
items.description: One of the largest palaces in Europe with over 3,000 rooms, grander than Versailles or Buckingham, where the Throne Room, Royal Armoury and Stradivarius collection dazzle. Private after-hours access can be arranged for discreet visits.

items.name: Catedral de la Almudena
items.description: Madrid's neo-Gothic cathedral faces the Royal Palace across the Plaza de la Armería, its brightly coloured modern ceiling a surprise inside a classical shell. Climb to the dome for a quiet rooftop panorama over the old town.

items.name: Parque del Buen Retiro (El Retiro)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: The city's green lung and former royal pleasure garden, made for rowing on the boating lake, strolling shaded avenues and letting children run free. Its rose garden and grand monuments reward a slow morning walk.

items.name: Palacio de Cristal del Retiro
items.description: A shimmering 1887 glass-and-iron pavilion set beside a pond in the Retiro, one of Madrid's most photographed structures. Note it is closed for restoration until around 2027, though its striking exterior, currently wrapped in Reina Sofía art interventions, is still worth the walk.

items.name: Plaza Mayor
items.description: The grand arcaded 17th-century square at the heart of Habsburg Madrid, ringed by frescoed facades and framed by nine stone archways. Best at early morning or evening when the day-trippers thin and the porticoes empty out.

items.name: Puerta del Sol
items.description: The symbolic centre of Spain, marked by the Kilometre Zero plaque from which all the country's roads are measured and the bear-and-strawberry-tree statue. A useful orienting point and the beating pulse of the city.

items.name: Gran Vía
items.description: Madrid's early-20th-century grand boulevard of belle-époque and art-deco towers, cinemas and rooftop bars, the 'Spanish Broadway'. Walk it at dusk when the facades light up, or catch a Spanish-language musical.

items.name: Mercado de San Miguel
items.description: A beautiful 1916 wrought-iron market turned gourmet food hall beside Plaza Mayor, where stalls run from Galician shellfish to Rodrigo de la Calle's Michelin-starred paella. Grazing here suits mixed groups and there are plenty of vegetable and cheese counters for veg-aware guests.

items.name: El Rastro
items.description: Spain's largest open-air flea market, spilling down La Latina's streets every Sunday morning with antiques, leather, prints and curios. Follow it with tapas and a vermouth in the surrounding taverns, a cherished local Sunday ritual.

items.name: Templo de Debod
items.description: A genuine 2nd-century-BC Egyptian temple, gifted to Spain and re-erected on a hill west of the centre, mirrored in a reflecting pool. It is Madrid's most romantic sunset spot, when the stones glow amber over the sierra.

items.name: Azotea del Círculo de Bellas Artes
items.description: The rooftop terrace of the century-old fine-arts club, 56 metres up, delivers a 360-degree sweep over Gran Vía, Cibeles and the tiled skyline. Come at golden hour with a cocktail for the most elegant view in the city.

items.name: Teatro Real (Royal Opera House)
items.description: Madrid's 1850 opera house, facing the Royal Palace, stages world-class opera and ballet under lavish gilt and superb acoustics. A private box turns an evening into an occasion for a family or a discreet party.

items.name: Corral de la Morería
credentials: MICHELIN Guide, Corral de la Morería Gastronómico, One Star
items.description: Widely regarded as the finest flamenco tablao in the world, hosting legendary dancers since 1956 in an intimate room where you dine as you watch. Its separate gastronomic space under chef David García holds a Michelin star, a rare pairing of art and haute cuisine.

items.name: Estadio Santiago Bernabéu
items.description: Real Madrid's newly rebuilt cathedral of football, where the Bernabéu Tour walks you onto the pitch, through the dressing room and past the trophy room. A thrill for children and lifelong fans; VIP and matchday hospitality can be arranged discreetly.

items.name: DiverXO
items.description: Chef Dabiz Muñoz's boundary-smashing tasting menu is the only three-Michelin-star table in Madrid and ranks among the world's top five restaurants. A theatrical, once-in-a-trip splurge; the kitchen accommodates dietary requests with advance notice.

items.name: Barrio de Salamanca, the Golden Mile
items.description: Madrid's most refined district, where Calle Serrano and Calle Ortega y Gasset line up Loewe, Chanel, Dior and Spain's finest ateliers amid grand 19th-century mansions. The natural base for luxury shopping and elegant, unhurried lunches.

items.name: Museo Sorolla
items.description: The preserved home, studio and Andalusian-inspired garden of Joaquín Sorolla, Spain's master of light, hung with over a thousand of his luminous canvases. A serene, intimate escape that feels worlds away from the tourist trail.

items.name: Museo Lázaro Galdiano
items.description: The former mansion of a financier-collector, four floors of Goya, El Greco, Zurbarán, jewellery and ivories displayed in opulent private-house rooms. One of Madrid's most rewarding hidden gems, rarely crowded.

items.name: Museo Cerralbo
items.description: A 19th-century aristocrat's palace frozen in time, its ballroom, chandeliers, tapestries and armour left exactly as the Marquis of Cerralbo arranged them. An intimate window into how Madrid's nobility once lived.

items.name: Real Jardín Botánico
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: An 18th-century royal botanical garden of some 5,000 plant species right beside the Prado, laid out in tranquil terraces and glasshouses. A calming green interval between museum visits, easy for elders and children.

items.name: Monasterio de las Descalzas Reales
items.description: A still-working convent of Franciscan nuns founded in 1559 in a former royal palace, concealing an astonishing hoard of tapestries, paintings and a frescoed grand staircase. Guided visits only, which keeps this treasure blissfully quiet.

items.name: Real Basílica de San Francisco el Grande
items.description: A neoclassical basilica crowned by one of the largest domes in Europe, its interior a gilded blaze of frescoes and canvases including an early Goya. Underrated and often near-empty despite its splendour.

items.name: Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida
items.description: A tiny hermitage whose dome Goya frescoed in 1798, and beneath which the painter himself is buried. A jewel-box of a stop, moving for anyone who has just seen his work in the Prado.

items.name: CaixaForum Madrid & Vertical Garden
items.description: A Herzog & de Meuron arts centre appearing to float above the street, fronted by a living wall of 15,000 plants, the first vertical garden in Spain. Ambitious rotating exhibitions make it a reliable cultural draw beside the Golden Triangle.

items.name: Barrio de las Letras (Literary Quarter)
items.description: The old haunt of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Spain's Golden Age writers, now a lattice of pedestrian lanes with literary quotes underfoot, wine bars and antique shops. A characterful stroll between the Prado and Puerta del Sol.

items.name: La Latina tapas crawl
items.description: Madrid's most atmospheric tapas district, its Cava Baja and Cava Alta streets packed with historic taverns pouring vermouth and plating croquetas and tortilla. Many kitchens do excellent vegetable and egg dishes, easy for veg-aware guests to graze happily.

items.name: Malasaña
items.description: The bohemian, design-forward barrio born of Madrid's 1980s countercultural Movida, now full of vintage boutiques, specialty coffee and independent galleries. A younger, creative counterpoint for teenagers and design lovers.

items.name: Chueca
items.description: Madrid's stylish, welcoming and famously vibrant quarter, dense with concept stores, terraces and some of the city's best modern restaurants around Mercado de San Antón. Lively yet easy, with rooftop dining that suits mixed groups.

items.name: Faro de Moncloa
items.description: A 92-metre observation tower with a glass-walled deck giving a clean, elevated panorama over the western parks, the sierra and the whole city grid. A quick, uncrowded way to grasp Madrid's layout on arrival.

items.name: Matadero Madrid
items.description: A vast former slaughterhouse reborn as a raw, buzzing contemporary-arts campus of cinemas, exhibition halls, design studios and theatre. A window into today's creative Madrid, and a striking piece of industrial reuse.

items.name: Madrid Río & Puente de Toledo
items.description: A riverside park reclaimed by burying the ring road, now a leafy ribbon of walkways, playgrounds and beach-fountains along the Manzanares. A relaxed, family-friendly counterpoint to the museums, best on foot or by bicycle.

items.name: Plaza de Cibeles & Palacio de Cibeles rooftop
items.description: The city's most iconic fountain and civic square, with the wedding-cake CentroCentro palace beside it offering a viewing terrace, Mirador Madrid, over the rooftops. The junction of the Paseo del Prado's grand ceremonial axis.

items.name: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando
items.description: A superb, blessedly quiet picture gallery holding Goyas, including his own self-portraits, plus Zurbarán, Rubens and El Greco, where the great painter once served as director. The connoisseur's alternative to the Prado's crowds.

items.name: El Corte Inglés Gourmet Experience, Callao
items.description: A top-floor food hall and terrace with a head-on view of the Gran Vía's illuminated Schweppes building and rooftops. Casual, high-energy and easy for a mixed-age group wanting a drink with a view.

items.name: Museo Arqueológico Nacional
items.description: Spain's national archaeology museum, whose star is the enigmatic Iberian sculpture the Lady of Elche, alongside Roman mosaics and Visigothic treasures. Beautifully modernised and rarely overwhelming, good for curious children.

items.name: Toledo
items.area: Day trip, approx. 70 km / 35 min by high-speed train
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic City of Toledo
items.description: A medieval hilltop city encircled by the Tagus where Christian, Muslim and Jewish worlds fused, home to El Greco's greatest works and a soaring Gothic cathedral. A private guide and car make an unforgettable full day; its whole historic city is a UNESCO site.

items.name: Segovia
items.area: Day trip, approx. 90 km / 30 min by high-speed train
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old Town of Segovia and its Aqueduct
items.description: A storybook town crowned by a Roman aqueduct of 20,000 mortar-free granite blocks and the turreted Alcázar that inspired Disney. Lunch on the region's famed roast, or lighter Castilian fare for veg-aware guests, before the drive back.

items.name: El Escorial (Real Monasterio de San Lorenzo)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Monastery and Site of the Escurial
items.description: Philip II's austere granite monastery-palace at the foot of the sierra, part royal mausoleum, part library, part basilica, and one of Spain's most powerful monuments. Cool mountain air and a grand setting make it an easy, rewarding half-day.

items.name: Aranjuez
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Aranjuez Cultural Landscape
items.description: A royal spring retreat of palaces and formal riverside gardens along the Tagus, all fountains, tree-lined avenues and 18th-century calm. Arrive on the vintage Strawberry Train in season for a gentle, multi-generational outing.

items.name: Alcalá de Henares
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, University and Historic Precinct of Alcalá de Henares
items.description: The world's first planned university city and Cervantes's birthplace, with a golden-stone historic quarter and Spain's most storied lecture halls. A cultured, easy escape that pairs literary heritage with excellent Castilian tapas.

items.name: Chinchón
items.description: A perfectly preserved medieval town built around a circular, galleried Plaza Mayor that doubles as a bullring, ringed by taverns pouring the local anís. A charming, off-the-beaten-track lunch stop far from the crowds.

items.name: DiverXO
items.description: Dabiz Muñoz's wild, world-beating three-star canvas, the most audacious tasting menu in Spain, and one of the greatest on earth.

items.name: Deessa
items.description: Quique Dacosta's Mediterranean haute cuisine in the Ritz's Belle Époque splendour, two stars beside the Prado.

items.name: Coque
items.description: The Sandoval brothers' theatre of a restaurant, a five-act journey from cellar to kitchen to table, held at two stars.

items.name: Paco Roncero Restaurante
items.description: Paco Roncero's avant-garde cooking inside the grand Casino de Madrid, technical, playful, two stars.

items.name: DSTAgE
items.description: Diego Guerrero's raw, industrial-chic room and free-thinking cooking, one of Madrid's most personal two-star tables.

items.name: Smoked Room
items.description: Dani García's fire-and-smoke haute cuisine, a small, intense counter built around the embers, at two stars.

items.name: Ramón Freixa Atelier
items.description: Ramón Freixa's signature cooking, back at two stars in an intimate new atelier, precise, considered, personal.

items.name: A'Barra
items.description: Product-driven cooking of real refinement, and a live-fire counter that is a show in itself.

items.name: El Invernadero
items.description: Rodrigo de la Calle's temple to the vegetable, 'gastrobotánica' cooking that puts produce centre-stage.

items.name: Saddle
items.description: Grand, gracious service and classical-contemporary cooking, a room that revived the art of the trolley and the table-side flourish.

items.name: Yugo the Bunker
items.area: Barrio de las Letras (Calle San Blas)
items.description: A Japanese-Spanish counter and a hidden 'bunker' below, Julián Mármol's cult sushi and kaiseki.

items.name: La Tasquería
items.description: Javi Estévez's ode to offal, the humblest cuts turned into something dazzling, and a star for the effort.

items.name: Clos Madrid
items.description: Marcos Granda's produce-led Mediterranean cooking and an exceptional cellar, a sommelier's restaurant.

items.name: Corral de la Morería Gastronómico
items.description: A tiny, four-table gastronomic room inside the world's great flamenco tablao, dinner and pure flamenco in one night.

items.name: Gaytán
items.description: Javier Aranda's minimalist room around an open kitchen, precise, seasonal cooking under a striking geometric ceiling.

items.name: Ricardo Sanz Wellington
items.description: The godfather of Spanish-Japanese fusion, Ricardo Sanz's nigiri and Mediterranean-inflected sushi at the Wellington.

items.name: RavioXO
items.description: Dabiz Muñoz's dumpling house, the DiverXO imagination poured into pasta and dumplings from around the world.

items.name: Ugo Chan
items.description: Hugo Muñoz's free-wheeling Spanish-Japanese cooking, one of the city's most exciting recent stars.

items.name: Desde 1911
items.description: A fish-house of extraordinary quality from a historic fishmonger, the finest seafood, treated with reverence.

items.name: Quimbaya
items.description: Edwin Rodríguez's refined Colombian cooking, the first star for a kitchen bringing South America to Madrid.

items.name: Cebo
items.area: Centro (Hotel Urban, Carrera de San Jerónimo)
items.description: Contemporary Spanish cooking with a Levantine hand, inside the design-led Hotel Urban.

items.name: Santerra
items.description: Miguel Carretero's cooking rooted in the Spanish countryside, game, croquetas and produce done seriously.

items.name: Gofio
items.area: Barrio de las Letras (Calle Lope de Vega)
items.description: Safe Cruz's tribute to Canary Islands cooking, a tiny room bringing the archipelago's produce and culture to Madrid.

items.name: OSA
items.description: A young couple's produce-led tasting menu by the river, tradition and innovation in a serene, out-of-the-way room.

items.name: Toki
items.description: Marcos Granda's intimate omakase counter, precise, seasonal Japanese cooking in a hushed, tiny room.

items.name: VelascoAbellá
items.description: Óscar Velasco and Montse Abellá's market-driven cooking, a first star for two of Spain's most respected hands.

items.name: La Tasquita de Enfrente
items.description: A beloved market-cuisine institution behind Gran Vía, Juanjo López's produce so good the menu changes by the morning.

items.name: Sobrino de Botín
credentials: Guinness World Record, world's oldest restaurant
items.description: The oldest restaurant on earth, open since 1725, cochinillo and cordero from the original wood-fired oven.

items.name: Tripea
items.description: Roberto Martínez Foronda's tiny market stall doing vivid Asian-Peruvian fusion, one of Madrid's most joyful tables.

items.name: Bacira
items.description: A trio of chefs weaving Mediterranean, Japanese and Peruvian threads, creative, generous, always full.

items.name: Kappo
items.description: Mario Payán's Japanese counter, an honest, affordable omakase and one of the city's best sushi seats for the price.

items.name: Casa Macareno
items.description: An old-fashioned Madrid tavern reborn, traditional Spanish cooking and a bar, done with real care.

items.name: Tepic
items.description: Honest, vibrant Mexican cooking in the heart of Chueca, a Bib Gourmand favourite for good, affordable food.

items.name: Taberna Pedraza
items.description: Classic Spanish taberna cooking of the highest order, the tortilla and croquetas that locals argue are the city's best.

items.name: Lakasa
items.area: Chamberí (Plaza del Descubridor Diego de Ordás)
items.description: César Martín's warm, produce-led cooking, an inventive neighbourhood room that has kept its Bib for years.

items.name: Gin Bar, Santo Mauro
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN One-Key hotel, a bar of real standing
items.description: An Art Deco cocktail bar in a duke's mansion, channelling old New York, the most discreet drink in the city.

items.name: Charrada, Four Seasons Madrid
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel, a bar of international standing
items.description: A polished cocktail bar inside the Four Seasons at Canalejas, expert drinks in the city's finest new luxury house.

items.name: Salmón Gurú
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 37), the highest-ranked bar in Madrid
items.description: Madrid's globally-ranked cocktail bar, Diego Cabrera's high-energy, comic-book den of bold, laboratory-made drinks.

items.name: Angelita Madrid
items.description: A dual wine bar and cocktail lab from the Villalón brothers, 500 labels upstairs, farm-to-glass drinks below.

items.name: Círculo de Bellas Artes, Azotea
credentials: Atop a Bien de Interés Cultural landmark, the city's most celebrated rooftop
items.description: The rooftop of Madrid's grand 1880s arts club, the definitive panorama over Gran Vía and the Metropolis dome.

items.name: Picalagartos Sky Bar
credentials: A landmark Gran Vía rooftop, atop the NH Collection Gran Vía
items.description: A sleek rooftop over the theatre-lit canyon of Gran Vía, cocktails with the city's grandest avenue at your feet.

items.name: Ginkgo Sky Bar
credentials: A landmark rooftop, atop the VP Plaza España Design hotel
items.description: A twelfth-floor rooftop and pool over Plaza de España, cocktails with the Royal Palace and Sierra beyond.

items.name: Palosanto, The Madrid EDITION
credentials: Atop a MICHELIN One-Key hotel, a destination rooftop
items.description: The EDITION's buzzy rooftop over the old centre, a pool, a scene and a considered drink under the Madrid sky.

plan.heading: 3 days in Madrid, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tour of the Prado at opening, focused on Velazquez, Goya and Bosch.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Reina Sofia for Picasso's Guernica, then a walk in the Retiro to the Crystal Palace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at DiverXO, Dabiz Munoz's three-Michelin room, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Royal Palace and its armoury, then the gardens and the neighbouring cathedral.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The lanes of the Barrio de Las Letras and Plaza Mayor, then jamon and sherry at a classic taberna.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitivo on the rooftop of the Hotel Riu or the Four Seasons Dani, then dinner at Santceloni or DSTAgE.

days.label: Day 3
days.title: Toledo and the tables of Madrid

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to Toledo for the Cathedral, El Greco's Burial of the Count of Orgaz, and the old Jewish quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return via lunch, then the Thyssen-Bornemisza to complete the Golden Triangle.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Coque, the Sandoval brothers' Michelin room, ending in its cellar.

items.name: Barrio de las Letras / Huertas
items.description: Literary, walkable and central, close to the Prado triangle; suits first-time visitors who want everything on foot.

items.name: Salamanca
items.description: The city's polished, moneyed grid of flagship boutiques and quiet streets; suits those who want calm and good shopping.

items.name: Malasaña / Chueca
items.description: Younger, design-led and lively after dark; suits travellers who want the bars and the buzz on their doorstep.

events.name: Fiestas de San Isidro
events.note: Madrid's patron-saint festival brings open-air verbenas, chotis dancing and concerts across the old city.

events.name: Mad Cool Festival
events.note: The city's major international music festival, held over four days at the Iberdrola Music grounds in Villaverde.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: The Barrio de Salamanca and the streets around the Prado are the refined places to stay; the city dines late, so reserve for 9:30pm or later, and reserve the Prado and Reina Sofia in advance.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Madrid Barajas (MAD), where a chauffeured car collects you and reaches the centre in around twenty-five minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The centre is walkable and the metro excellent; a discerning traveller keeps a private driver for the museums, evenings and day trips to Toledo or Segovia.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong 5G citywide; a Spain or EU eSIM works instantly and hotel wifi is reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards and contactless are standard, carry a little cash for tapas bars and taxis, and tipping is light with rounding up considered generous.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-June and September-October are ideal: warm, dry, clear. Avoid July-August, when the high plateau bakes past 35 C and locals leave the city, and the coldest snaps of January.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India. Air India flies Delhi-Madrid one-stop; cleaner premium routings are one-stop via Gulf hubs (Qatar via Doha, Emirates via Dubai, Etihad via Abu Dhabi) or via European hubs into Madrid Barajas (~12-14h total). Qatar Qsuite via Doha is the strongest business cabin; Barajas Terminal 4S handles most one-world/Iberia arrivals, so match your hub to your onward cabin.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine EU standards. One of Europe's safer capitals; ordinary big-city pickpocketing on the metro and around Sol/Gran Via is the main caution. Tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Workable for vegetarians though Spanish cuisine is meat-heavy, so choose venues deliberately; Jain needs clear briefing (garlic, jamon and fish stock are pervasive). Good Indian options, e.g. Benares and Swagat, plus dedicated vegetarian spots like Vega and El Huerto de Lucas.
